title: The Met’s Other Failure
excerpt: The Metropolitan Museum of Art’s announcement this week that it is canceling next year’s exhibition on the fashion of John Galliano perhaps shouldn’t have come
body: The Metropolitan Museum of Art’s announcement this week that it is canceling next year’s exhibition on the fashion of John Galliano perhaps shouldn’t have come as a surprise
From the start, Galliano was a controversial pick for the museum’s Costume Institute, which launches its new show each year with the splashy Met Gala

In 2011, he lost his job as creative director of Dior after a video surfaced of him making a drunken anti-Semitic rant; later that year, a French court found him guilty of the crime of making anti-Semitic and anti-Asian insults

The New York Times also recently described claims that Galliano had made anti-Semitic comments during an outburst in 2019. (Through a spokesperson, Galliano denied the 2019 episode.) But not long after his Dior exit, Galliano—who has always traded on his bad-boy image while producing clothes of astounding beauty and theatricality—was welcomed back into the industry
After so publicly hitting rock-bottom, the designer, who said addiction to drugs and alcohol led to the rants, apologized and went to rehab
Celebrities such as Zendaya wore his designs; this year, the fast-fashion retailer Zara announced a partnership with him to great excitement
Anna Wintour, Vogue ’s global editorial director and the Met Gala’s chair, also happens to be his longtime friend and champion

In the process of planning the Met show, Galliano, Wintour, and Andrew Bolton, the Costume Institute’s curator, consulted with Jewish leaders, and the exhibition itself intended to—as the museum initially announced in July—explore how the designer’s “derogatory conduct” had “fundamentally altered his career and public reception.” [ Read: Yet another wasted Met Gala ] Those efforts did little to assuage wider public opinion

Museum donors threatened to pull funding; the speaker of the New York city council called the choice of Galliano a “serious mistake.” On Monday, the museum released a statement saying that the show “will not proceed as planned.” It was, Wintour said in the statement, “the right decision.” It is also a blow to the museum and its reputation that could have been avoided

For most of the Costume Institute’s 80-year history, it has followed an unofficial rule: Don’t do a solo show about a living designer—because such an exhibition could be seen as a form of advertising instead of scholarship, especially if the designer has curatorial input

Although such shows are now commonplace, the Met’s fashion wing has always prided itself on “setting the standard” for conservation and collection, and has devoted only two exhibitions to living designers: Yves Saint Laurent in 1983 and Rei Kawakubo in 2017
Both were controversial exceptions to long-standing norms intended to separate cultural analysis from commercialism

Putting on a museum exhibition of Galliano’s work, even while interrogating his past behavior, was always going to be ethically dicey because the designer still stands to benefit from the publicity and prestige that the show bestows
This saga suggests that the Costume Institute, and perhaps all fashion museums, should forgo retrospectives of living artists—and revisit why rules discouraging them were necessary to begin with
Museums have been routinely collecting and displaying clothes as a branch of the decorative arts since the 19th century, but early fashion exhibits typically featured only historical dress
Contemporary fashion was considered insufficiently artistic, and highlighting it was seen as overly promotional
But as fashion designers became household names in the 1960s, more contemporary pieces found their way into thematic exhibitions
Usually, the items were in shows featuring the work of several designers, including at the Met, which minimized the appearance of endorsing a particular label

The Costume Institute, which opened to the public in 1946, didn’t devote an entire show to an individual living designer until 1983, when Diana Vreeland—a former Vogue editor in chief—curated a retrospective of Yves Saint Laurent’s work in honor of his label’s 25th anniversary
Saint Laurent was involved in the exhibition and attended the opening fundraiser, both of which were underwritten by the firm that had long designed his textiles
Critics argued that it canonized a designer whose work had not yet stood the test of time, while blurring the boundary between art and advertising

The general public, though, was clearly captivated: The show drew more than 125,000 visitors in just its first month at a time when the average Met exhibition drew 500,000 visitors a year, Women’s Wear Daily reported
Despite its popularity, the experiment was not repeated under the next curator, or the next

Indeed, the Times later reported that the Costume Institute had adopted an “unofficial policy” of not doing monographic shows on living designers due to the “charges of commercialism” that the exhibition drew
Designers, however, took note of the public’s growing interest in fashion heritage and realized that their own histories could be a valuable source of design inspiration and cultural capital
In 1987, Dior created an archives department; most major fashion labels followed
Fashion-industry archivists started competing with museum curators to buy back their own vintage pieces at auction
Some fashion houses founded their own museums

Others turned their archives into touring exhibitions, large on spectacle and light on scholarship. [ Read: Confessions of a costume curator ] By no coincidence, over the course of the 1990s, fashion studies gained traction as an academic discipline. “Suddenly, fashion was about identity, the body, gender, power, and visual representation,” Valerie Steele, a fashion historian and curator, wrote in Reinvention and Restlessness , a book created for an exhibition at the Museum at FIT
Fashion not only explained the past, the thinking went, but also expressed the ambitions and anxieties of the present

But the mingling of intellectual analysis and business interests hasn’t occurred without debate: Privately owned objects aren’t subject to the same strict conservation requirements as museum artifacts

And as museums started borrowing archival pieces directly from fashion houses, sometimes a designer’s “cooperation” with an exhibition stretched to input or approval—another ethical gray area that can compromise curatorial objectivity and authority
The ethics of fashion exhibitions got even more questionable in 2000, when the Guggenheim mounted a show about the Italian designer Giorgio Armani

The museum, which does not collect fashion, received a $15 million donation from the designer; the move was widely viewed as a transparent quid pro quo. “It’s all very well for an art gallery to declare the equality of ‘high’ and ‘low’ art forms, and to enjoy the boost in attendance that may bring,” one critic wrote at the time, “but the challenges and risks of shows like this can outweigh any benefits.” Whether they’re focused on pants or paintings, museum exhibitions don’t just publicize and promote the work of living artists; their imprimatur actually raises its market value
The Armani show had the distinction of prompting a museum-industry trade group and the IRS to update their ethical guidelines on corporate sponsorship to encourage greater transparency
Still, shows about living designers—produced with the help of those designers—became more common, and eventually they lost much of their stigma
For many years, in fact, the Met was one of the few holdouts
Its policy changed only when Bolton became curator in charge in 2016 and announced a show on the Japanese designer Rei Kawakubo

Bolton, according to a Times report , explicitly “wanted to challenge the idea” that museums couldn’t do monographs on living designers, and wanted to “demonstrate that ‘fashion is a living art.’” Kawakubo’s involvement was crucial to the museum’s show; every piece came from her archives, and that year, she served as the honorary chair for the Met Gala
Galliano, with his past behavior, complicates the ethics equation even more

title: The MAGA Right Is Only Pretending to Be Censored
excerpt: F or nearly a year and a half, the Trump administration prepared its case
body: F or nearly a year and a half, the Trump administration prepared its case
Political appointees inside the State Department combed through old files and databases
Civil servants received notice that their personal emails would be examined

Darren Beattie—the founder of a far-right conspiracist website, then the undersecretary of state for public diplomacy—sent out a request for files on anyone who had communicated with or written about the Global Engagement Center, a now-dissolved agency that once worked to expose propaganda campaigns by Russia, China, Iran, and other countries around the world. [ Read: The white nationalist in charge of Trump’s public diplomacy ] The request, seen last year by the MIT Technology Review , was far-reaching

Beattie was seeking information on Bill Gates; the commentator Bill Kristol; Chris Krebs, a former U.S. cybersecurity official; a German government minister; the analyst Renée DiResta, formerly at Stanford University, as well as others associated with a research project called the Election Integrity Partnership; and, as it happens, me
This unprecedented investigation was meant to expose the Biden administration’s “censorship–industrial complex,” a shadowy network allegedly dedicated to the mass suppression of American free speech
Since 2020, internet trolls have accused Biden-administration officials, social-media companies, and university researchers of weaving a nefarious plot to censor conservatives
Since 2025, MAGA ideologues have been using this alleged plot as an excuse to dismantle government programs, stifle research, intimidate American citizens, and even distort American foreign policy
And yet for the past year and half, neither Beattie nor anyone else has actually managed to prove that the plot ever existed
Like a soap bubble that vanishes with the touch of a hand, the “censorship–industrial complex” belongs to that mystical category of things that disappear when you examine them too closely
The failure to produce evidence is not for lack of trying
During the Biden administration, MAGA allies and politicians filed multiple lawsuits with the goal of exposing alleged censorship
One of them, brought by the Missouri attorney general, made it all the way to the Supreme Court before justices asked for underlying evidence that the government had censored anyone

Another, brought against the Stanford research project by America First Legal—Stephen Miller’s team—failed in July, when a judge found the suit had no standing, no jurisdiction, and, after a discovery process requested by the plaintiffs, no evidence
There was no proof, in other words, that the Stanford research had resulted in anyone being censored

Other cases against the Biden administration were simply settled by President Trump’s Department of Justice without finding any evidence of “censorship” either. [ Renée DiResta: My encounter with the fantasy–industrial complex ] Now the Trump administration’s most dedicated ideologues have also failed, spectacularly, to prove the existence of a “censorship–industrial complex” inside the State Department

After months of searching, Beattie’s successor as undersecretary for public diplomacy, Sarah Rogers, recently decided to publicize the unimpressive results of the inquiry into the Global Engagement Center
But instead of writing a report admitting that the documents that surfaced contained nothing of interest, she leaked them, selectively, to an internet troll known as DataRepublican

Here is where the story becomes especially convoluted, and I will simplify as best I can. “DataRepublican” is the X pseudonym of Jennica Pounds, who has a history of misreading data and connecting dots to describe nonexistent conspiracies
But the plan went wrong: Upon receipt of raw documents from Rogers, including screenshots without context, Pounds decided that Rogers was a “Deep State” operative and refused to release them
Subsequently, it emerged that Pounds herself has been secretly employed by the Pentagon, which presumably makes her a deep-state operative too
Because Pounds would not publish the documents, Rogers did so herself, in a long thread on X
As she must have known, they contained no evidence of conspiracy, no proof that anyone in the Biden administration censored millions or even dozens of social-media posts
Instead, Rogers, who is theoretically responsible for promoting good relations with people in foreign countries, went after a series of U.S. citizens
She found a GEC official who had about a dozen email exchanges with the Stanford project, almost all about Russian accounts

She posted a brief excerpt of the congressional testimony of Daniel Kimmage, a former State Department employee and GEC deputy coordinator, who truthfully explained that the center was set up to deal with foreign disinformation, not American media
Rogers wrote that “that was a lie,” without offering proof

Rogers also included several misleading posts about the Stanford project, plucking a number from a table and implying that it meant the researchers had somehow targeted more than 400,000 tweets, when they in fact had merely noted their existence
More to the point, the Stanford team did so after the election , not in some kind of smoke-filled room but in an academic report that is still publicly available and that DiResta has cited repeatedly

Rogers also criticized another very public, not remotely secret report, written jointly by the United States, Britain, Canada, Germany, Slovakia, and the European Union, investigating “gendered disinformation,” a subject that sounds very “woke” until you realize that deepfake porn videos and orchestrated misogyny are tactics regularly used against female politicians such as Annalena Baerbock, a former German foreign minister, or Giorgia Meloni, the Italian prime minister
The Iranian regime uses them to harass female dissidents around the world
Democratic governments would be negligent if they did not try to understand them

But even if you are not bothered by the online harassment of women in politics, it’s still impossible to argue that the publication of a report (and its translation into nine languages) proves the existence of a secret censorship–industrial complex stifling Americans’ views. “Watergate it was not,” Orna Blum, a former State Department official, wrote last week. [ Anne Applebaum: America surrenders in the information wars ] And if the scandal wasn’t Watergate, Rogers is not Bob Woodward

She is a public servant who dumped raw data online, seemingly without asking whether anyone would be damaged or which American foreign-policy interests could be served, all in the name of proving nothing
I n the normal course of things the saga of the GEC documents would be, and should be, dismissed as a storm in a teapot
But unfortunately, the administration’s pursuit of a nonexistent censorship–industrial complex has already had real consequences for real people

In April 2025, Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced that he was closing the Global Engagement Center because it had “spent millions of dollars to actively silence and censor the voices of Americans they were supposed to be serving.” This was untrue, and even at the time there was no evidence for such an extraordinary statement

On the contrary, the GEC was the only institution in the U.S. government that was publicly tracking hostile international information operations, including by exposing websites in Africa or Latin America that appeared local but were in fact run by Moscow or Beijing
Rubio’s statement maligned the people who worked on these reports
Will the secretary of state now apologize to them? Compensate them? Rehire them? The closing of the center also means that no one is now doing that work

title: How Trump Lost Asia
excerpt: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube In this episode of The David Frum Show , The Atlantic ’s David Frum opens with a discussion of how Donald Tru
body: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube In this episode of The David Frum Show , The Atlantic ’s David Frum opens with a discussion of how Donald Trump has enriched himself and his family during his presidencies
David discusses how these ill-gotten gains bring up difficult questions about the future of American democracy

Then David is joined by former Australian Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull to discuss the impact of the Trump presidency on America’s allies, its reputation around the world, and the politics in the Pacific
Finally, David ends the episode with a discussion of Red Dawn Over China: How Communism Conquered a Quarter of Humanity , by Frank Dikötter

The following is a transcript of the episode: Malcolm Turnbull: T he United States—not by accident or circumstance, but by design—has become a less dependable ally. [ Music ] David Frum: Hello, and welcome to The David Frum Show
I’m David Frum, a staff writer at The Atlantic

My guest this week will be former Australian Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull, and we will discuss the deterioration of the position, the strategic and economic position, of the Western democracies in the Indian Ocean and Pacific Ocean in the presidencies of Donald Trump
The book this week will be Red Dawn Over China: How Communism Conquered a Quarter of Humanity
But before either the dialogue with Malcolm Turnbull or the book discussion, some opening thoughts about the question of President Trump’s wealth and what is to happen to it after he leaves office
I wrote about this subject in The Atlantic this past weekend, and you can see my thoughts there in much more elaborated form
But there’s some major themes that I think really need to be stressed again in a very direct way, and I’d like to do that here with you now

President Trump entered office in January 2025 as a wealthy man, as he has been almost all of his life: thanks to the great inheritance from his father, thanks to his earnings from The Apprentice and other TV programs, and thanks to some of his own business achievements
But his own business career has been one of sharp ups and downs, punctuated by bankruptcies of the businesses that he’s owned, losses to his investors
But there’s no question that he and his family are very, very wealthy today, with a fortune numbered in the multiple billions of dollars, accumulated in an astonishingly short time
How exactly did he do that? Well, as I read it, there are three major streams of payments that he has received; three major sources of wealth that he’s received since he became president
The first takes the form of payments from people, governments, and entities with interests before the United States government
He has, for example, received large payments from American media companies
Famously, the payment from Amazon to make a documentary of his wife, Melania
Settlements from Paramount , Meta , and ABC News, money that will supposedly go to his presidential library
He’s received gifts from foreign governments and entities as well
This stream of payments and gifts, worth many millions of dollars, has made Trump a rich man by any standard
The second source of wealth to him has been his involvement in the cryptocurrency and other crypto-token markets, where the president has backed cryptocurrency-issuing companies
Many of the currencies and tokens that have been issued by these Trump-backed companies rapidly became worthless
The third source has been a series of stock and other transactions in oil markets and other markets
This year, the president’s investment accounts, which the White House says are managed by third-party financial institutions, have traded oil and gas stocks
This has happened even as the president is deeply involved in the war in Iran, which has certainly had impact on this industry
Now, America has a long tradition of letting bygones be bygones and of not looking very deeply at the activities of former presidents
But the enormous fortune that has been accumulated in such dubious ways in such a short time raises important questions
Not just about right and wrong, not just about whether individual economic laws have been obeyed, but important questions about the future of American democracy
There are examples all over the planet of authoritarian rulers whose families accumulated enormous wealth in their time in office

The authoritarian ruler then loses power; some of the fortune is clawed back, but much is kept by the family, and that fortune becomes a basis for the family’s return to political power in a new generation
We’ve seen that in Peru with the Fujimori dynasty, in the Philippines with the Marcos dynasty
Could we see such a thing in America? You know, the next generation of Trumps are going to inherit a lot of money, but they’re going to also inherit a lot of potential legal vulnerabilities

And one of the lessons they’ve learned from the presidency of Donald Trump is: When you have a large fortune with such a big question mark over it, one way to be safe is to reclaim political power and shut down investigations and law enforcement and accountability
And that way, the money that you achieved, whatever question marks are about it, well—no questions can be asked, because there’s no one to ask the questions

While this enormous accumulation, rapid accumulation, of uncertain wealth remains, it continues as not just a question mark over the future of the Trump family, but a question mark over the future of American democracy
It’s a risk in a way that the wealth of the Fujimoris in Peru has been a risk, in a way that the wealth of the Marcos in the Philippines has been a risk
Americans are not a backward-looking people

In the Biden presidency, pretty clearly, Attorney General Merrick Garland wanted to stay well away from the whole Trump business, and to leave Trump as much alone as Trump’s record would possibly allow Merrick Garland to leave Trump alone

But if there is a post-Trump administration that is concerned to restore American democracy, I don’t think that kind of averting-the-eyes method that was practiced by Merrick Garland and President Biden is safe or sustainable

title: The Court’s Ballroom Decision Is a Sign of Deeper Problems
excerpt: In deciding to allow President Trump to proceed with constructing a new ballroom, which Congress has not authorized, at the White House, which Trump does not ow
body: In deciding to allow President Trump to proceed with constructing a new ballroom, which Congress has not authorized, at the White House, which Trump does not own, the U.S
Supreme Court invoked the separation of powers

But the Court got the constitutional problem precisely backwards: The separation-of-powers problem isn’t that courts are impermissibly blocking the president’s use of taxpayer funds to create a ballroom
It’s that the president is impermissibly using unauthorized taxpayer funds to create a ballroom

The Court’s missteps were many, starting in the very first sentence of its opinion : “In October 2025, the federal government started a project to replace the East Wing of the White House.” (The opinion, decided via the Court’s shadow docket, was per curiam, meaning that it did not indicate an author, but because the four dissenters noted their names, we know the five justices in the majority were Clarence Thomas, Samuel Alito, Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh, and Amy Coney Barrett.) But the federal government didn’t begin replacing part of the White House
Only the president and the executive branch did
Constitution, the president is not the be-all and end-all of the federal government
Far from it: The legislature, Congress, is the body that has the power to establish and regulate federal property (including the White House) and to authorize the spending of federal funds

Indeed, the plaintiff in the case—the National Trust for Historic Preservation in the United States—argued that the president was proceeding without congressional authorization and in violation of federal laws
The Supreme Court majority did not say otherwise, making no claim as to whether the ballroom-construction project was legal or whether the president had the authority to undertake it

The Supreme Court’s conflation of the president with the federal government is the latest iteration in the Court’s steady embrace of the unitary-executive theory and the accompanying expansion of executive power
This theory maintains that all executive power resides in the president, and that Congress cannot limit the president’s exercise of that power
Yet these days, the president, occasionally with the Court’s blessing, is claiming to possess legislative powers too
That is the case when the president declines to spend funds that Congress has obligated or when the president decides to spend funds that Congress has not authorized
Under the Constitution, Congress, not the president, has the power of the purse

Nevertheless, the unitary-executive theory unites all government power in the president, paving the way for an executive unbound by law. [ Alexandra Petri: A ballroom would have solved this ] The Court’s errors continued as justices attempted to explain why the lower courts were wrong to block the president’s demolition of a portion of the White House
The Court relied on the doctrine of standing, which maintains that a plaintiff challenging the government’s actions must show that they have been injured by the actions they are contesting

In this case, one of the members of the National Trust for Historic Preservation, who lives in Washington, D.C., and about once a month visits the neighborhood where the White House is located, alleged that she had “aesthetic, cultural, and historical interests” in what happened there
Under the Court’s precedents, that injury should have sufficed

Indeed, in a prior opinion by Justice Antonin Scalia, the Court had said that desire to “observe an animal species, even for purely esthetic purposes,” can constitute “a cognizable interest for purpose of standing.” Crocodiles and all animals are great and important, to be sure

As Chief Justice John Roberts wrote in his dissent, “The White House is not just any building.” It is “an iconic American building whose symbolism and history are wrapped up in its architecture.” The doctrine of standing, the Court has said, is a vital component of the separation of powers, because it ensures that the judicial branch stays within its role rather than encroaching on the other branches, specifically the executive
But in this case, as in others, the Court has invoked the doctrine to support the flow of power in one direction only: limiting Congress’s authority while expanding the president’s

In the ballroom case, the Court said the National Trust member did not have standing to sue, and therefore the plaintiff (and the federal courts) could not enforce the federal statutes that the president was allegedly violating
Following the decision, it’s unclear who, if anyone, can sue to enforce the federal laws that the plaintiffs allege the president is violating with the ballroom-construction project
That is the effect of many of the Court’s standing cases—to render congressional statutes unenforceable

Ramirez , the Court said that a group of plaintiffs who were incorrectly designated as suspected drug traffickers and terrorists in their credit reports could not sue to enforce Fair Credit Reporting Act provisions requiring consumer-reporting agencies to maintain accurate records
As a result of that decision, the FCRA provisions go largely unenforced

National Wildlife Federation , the Court said that plaintiffs seeking to enforce the Endangered Species Act and the Federal Land Policy and Management Act, among other laws, did not have standing, and thus could not enforce those laws either

Far from ensuring the separation of powers, the Court has used standing to undermine the principle: According to the Constitution, Congress has the power to make laws, but the Court’s standing decisions have freed the executive branch (and other entities) from having to comply with them
The Court made its final error in its analysis of the relevant harms in the case

To obtain emergency relief on the shadow docket, the party seeking relief (here, the president, as he was appealing the lower court’s injunction) is supposed to show that they would suffer irreparable harm if the Court does not act
The Court said the president is irreparably harmed because the lower court overstepped its powers, and undermined the separation of powers, by blocking the president’s actions
But if the president’s actions are illegal, it is more than a little odd to say that stopping them injures the president

That would essentially mean that at least some limits on the president’s power are unenforceable, because enforcing them would injure the president. [ Duncan Hosie: The Supreme Court isn’t interested in facts ] This is not the first decision to raise that harrowing implication

In a 2025 nationwide injunction case related to the birthright-citizenship executive order, the Court said the president was irreparably harmed because the lower courts had blocked an executive order—later determined to be unconstitutional—on a nationwide basis

Similarly, in the recent mail-in-ballot decision , the Court said the president was irreparably harmed because lower courts had blocked an executive order—one that is likely illegal—too soon, and before the plaintiffs experienced an injury
It is fine and good to ensure that lower courts are acting within the bounds of their authority
But the separation of powers demands that the Supreme Court stop undermining Congress’s power to make meaningful laws by allowing the executive to violate them without consequence.

title: The White House Wants to Make the Smithsonian a Pariah
excerpt: The Trump administration’s latest strategy to control the Smithsonian has the logic of lunchroom bullying; the Department of Interior is channeling “you can’t s
body: The Trump administration’s latest strategy to control the Smithsonian has the logic of lunchroom bullying; the Department of Interior is channeling “you can’t sit with us” energy as it tries to make the world’s largest museum complex a pariah in Washington

In a newly public August 28 letter from the department to the Smithsonian board of regents, Trump-administration officials write that executive departments and agencies “cannot in good conscience continue to support the Smithsonian under current leadership” and suggest that they cease cooperation with the Smithsonian on routine logistical matters, such as loaning items for exhibits and awarding discretionary grants

The letter was sent just days before the regents, having failed to secure an open site on the National Mall for the Smithsonian’s newest museums, resorted to placing the National Museum of the American Latino in a largely vacant building it already owns
In doing so, the Smithsonian dodged Congress, a move that reflects the inward turn of an institution on the outs

Such developments illustrate the growing alienation the Smithsonian faces in the capital and difficulties that go deeper than the superficial signage Donald Trump wants placed in front of one of its museums to discredit it

For the past year and a half, the White House has repeatedly threatened the institution, but recently, more parties have joined the effort—first Republicans in Congress who in two hearings scrutinized the National Museum of American History over supposed partisan bias, and now the Interior Department, which has no official oversight of the Smithsonian
Although partially government-funded, the Smithsonian is independent of the executive branch—the White House has essentially no say over what it does—and it was designed to be as such
Still, it’s becoming clear that functioning freely in this charged climate might also mean going it alone

Invoking the White House’s recent report on the Museum of American History, the Interior letter accuses the Smithsonian of potentially violating federal antidiscrimination laws—a common way, on the right, of criticizing DEI programs, especially those created in response to the racial-justice protests of the late 2010s and early 2020s

Signed by Interior Secretary Doug Burgum and Assistant to the President for Domestic Policy Vince Haley, the letter also requests a meeting with the board of regents, the entity that actually oversees the institution
The regents’ membership has been shrinking this year as members’ terms have ended and their positions have gone unfilled, reportedly due to administration pressure

Despite the language in the letter, a White House official told me by email that the Interior Department did not mean that agencies shouldn’t cooperate with the Smithsonian; rather, those agencies will “find it difficult to cooperate with current Smithsonian leadership in light of the disturbing evidence that has been uncovered.” The official also said it’s up to the Justice Department to determine whether the Smithsonian violated antidiscrimination laws and not to conflate “evidence of unlawful discrimination with a direct allegation that it happened.” In the letter, the Interior Department writes that institution leadership has embraced “radical ideology” that serves to “weaken our shared American identity” and “erase our heritage.” The rhetoric is particularly striking coming from the department at the center of contested efforts to take down wall texts at National Park sites across the country, where information on slavery, climate change, Native Americans, and other topics has been removed over the past year

The National Park Service represents a discomfiting alternate reality for the Smithsonian—one in which exhibits have been subject to political approval. [ Read: The Smithsonian’s show trial on Capitol Hill ] The White House is surely pleased with such changes at the National Park sites, which Trump called for in the same March 2025 executive order that kicked off the administration’s campaign against the Smithsonian

It seems to want to extend that kind of control to the museums on the National Mall, which Trump has asserted are too negative and focus too much on “how bad slavery was.” But with a president-proof system standing in officials’ way, they’ve had to seek out additional levers of pressure against Smithsonian leadership

The Interior letter represents the department’s most comprehensive public statement on the Smithsonian after the White House tapped it in July to place signs on National Park Service–controlled land outside the National Museum of American History, which will detail its alleged political biases and direct would-be visitors to what the administration describes as more accurate information
Much of this effort is about framing U.S. history in a more positive light, which the Smithsonian says it already does while also dealing with that history’s complexities
These partisan feuds are especially familiar to the Museum of the American Latino, which was subject to politicized scrutiny long before Trump started taking on the wider institution

Foreshadowing present criticisms, a 2022 Heritage Foundation op-ed described one of the museum’s early shows as a disgrace with an “unabashedly Marxist portrayal of history, religion and economics.” Writers for the right-wing think tank asserted that the museum should be defunded, a call one of them repeated this summer (and he threw in the Women’s History Museum for good measure)
The Museum of the American Latino’s placement in the Smithsonian’s Arts and Industries Building will surely disappoint some: No starchitect to deliver a glossy new design
No bespoke architecture, like the Museum of the American Indian’s sinuous facade or the Museum of African American History and Culture’s Yoruba-crown-inspired exterior
Then again, the World’s Fair–style building is arguably the loudest, most colorful structure on the National Mall
It certainly won’t look like a museum that anyone is trying to hide.

title: Facilitating AI integration with simplicity at scale
excerpt: As companies scale, the technology supporting operations can become a liability just as quickly as it becomes an asset
body: As companies scale, the technology supporting operations can become a liability just as quickly as it becomes an asset

Disconnected systems, site-specific tools, spreadsheets, and manual workarounds can create data silos that make it harder to spot problems early, coordinate responses, and make decisions with confidence
For Jabil, a global manufacturing company with more than 100 sites across more than 30 countries, the answer has been to make integration and simplification a priority

The company adopted a “simplify-first, then-innovate mindset,” says Harish Manohar, SAP IT director at Jabil, recognizing that adding new technologies without first reducing complexity risks creating more risk

The goal is to standardize processes, consolidate where possible, and establish a more consistent data backbone across the organization. “Any innovation without simplification is going to add more complexity,” Manohar says
That philosophy also changes how Jabil approaches modernization. “Any modernization or transformation should add measurable business value,” Manohar says
The company is focused on connecting processes end-to-end across its supply chain and creating a foundation that can scale consistently across regions

Integration comes first because, as Manohar puts it, “the backbone of any contemporary or modern organization is data.” Before organizations can optimize, automate, or apply AI, data needs to flow seamlessly across systems
But doing that across a global organization is hardly straightforward
Jabil’s more than 100 sites operate with different levels of process maturity, legacy systems, and localized workflows, while regulated businesses bring additional compliance requirements
As such, standardizing across different regions and business environments means changing processes and governance without disrupting the operations already in place
The value of that work extends beyond the technology to the people using it
Integrated workflows can offer employees shared visibility into data, reduce manual data reconciliation, and help them move from chasing information to acting on insights
For Jabil, the aim is also to improve real-time visibility into supply chain events, which can enable faster responses to disruptions and reduce operational risk
Looking to the future, that foundation could make AI and automation all the more useful and scalable
With trusted data and integrated systems in place, Jabil is exploring predictive supply chain insights, intelligent exception handling, and AI-driven planning and forecasting
To Manohar, the takeaway is clear: “Simplicity at scale is a very competitive advantage,” and technology investments must ultimately connect to business value and operational resilience
This episode of Business Lab is produced in partnership with SAP

Full Transcript: Megan Tatum: From MIT Technology Review, I’m Megan Tatum, and this is Business Lab, the show that helps business leaders make sense of new technologies coming out of the lab and into the marketplace
Our topic today is enterprise technology integration, and how the benefits of consolidating tools and systems across the supply chain help organizations operate more reliably at scale
When companies reduce tool sprawl and connect their systems more effectively, they gain earlier visibility, faster response, and greater resilience across production lines
My guest today is Harish Manohar, SAP IT Director at Jabil

Jabil has been on a journey to simplify its technology landscape by using SAP Integration Suite as the foundation to connect systems, retire fragmented tools, and enable more consistent operations globally
This podcast is produced in partnership with SAP
Megan: Thank you so much for being here, Harish
Just to start, if we could set some context, can you give us a quick overview of Jabil, the business and its overall transformation journey? Harish: All right
Jabil is a global manufacturing company headquartered in St
We have about 60 years of experience offering comprehensive engineering, supply chain, and manufacturing solutions across different industries
We have a global footprint of about over 100 different sites across 30-plus countries, 140,000-plus employees
We are a trusted partner for more than 400 of the world’s top brands
And a lot of scale there, as you’re referring to some of the stats there

As things have got more complex, where did disconnected tools and systems start to slow you down, and what ultimately drove you to make integration a really strategic priority? Harish: I talked about our global footprint across 100-plus sites
With a global footprint always comes complexity about site-specific tools
All of our sites have been in business for a long time, and over the period of years, they had their own tools for their own processes

When we are looking to scale, the first thing we wanted to start looking at is what is this mix of site-specific tools, manual workarounds, spreadsheet-based processes, legacy applications, whatnot? That’s a big technical debt that we have had over the last 25 years

That’s where we started, and that is what led Jabil to make integration a strategic priority because we had limited ability to see issues early across plants, across regions, which would help us to coordinate responses consistently, and also to be able to scale those responses consistently
This complexity created data silos, and in a way delayed robust decision-making
As the complexity increased globally, integration became extremely critical to a few things
It was critical to establishing a single trusted data backbone, which would directly enable faster coordinated responses across the network

We at Jabil, as part of our transformation journey, believe that having the right data at the right time fundamentally changes how we respond to disruptions, which is all about a manufacturing business

Can you fare any better? Puzzles and games have always been central to AI development
The term “machine learning” was popularized in a 1959 article about an algorithm that learned to play checkers
Judged purely on its puzzling skills, AI is improving a lot—and quickly
In late 2024, even the best models could figure out only 18% of the infamous New York Times Connections puzzles; by early 2025, some could solve them nearly perfectly every time
But puzzles do more than highlight AI’s progress
Seeing where models succeed and fail, and where humans still beat them, offers a window into the technology’s strengths and weaknesses
We’ve gathered seven puzzles that have stumped models at one time or another—now it’s your turn to see how you fare
Take our test to find out whether you can outsmart AI .  —Grace Huckins This article is from our latest print magazine, which is all about kids

How AI plotted an interstellar journey to Alpha Centauri A nonprofit organization called the Fermi Explorer Mission announced yesterday that it intends to launch a spacecraft to our nearest star system by the end of 2029
It’s a hugely ambitious mission—if all goes well, the spacecraft could take up to 80,000 years to arrive at Alpha Centauri, which is 4.4 light-years away
To get there, it will follow a novel trajectory discovered by an AI system developed by PSI, a physics research lab

Explore how AI found a new route to Alpha Centauri—and what the mission could tell us about alien life . —Michelle Kim MIT Technology Review Narrated: the role of the astronaut is in flux We go to space for geopolitical prestige, manifest destiny, spiritual fulfillment, scientific curiosity, and, increasingly, business opportunities

Weibel frames human space exploration as part of our need to embark on pilgrimages

title: Yosemite, again in corporate crosshairs, embodies the long war over US national park privatization
url:
<title>Yosemite, again in corporate crosshairs, embodies the long war over US national park privatization</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757349/original/file-20260901-50-qkwnev.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C5300%2C3533&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Yosemite National Park is home to three groves of massive ancient sequoia trees.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/yosemite-national-park-california-trees-named-the-bachelor-news-photo/2207354590">Jim West/UCG/Universal Images Group via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Reports that the Trump administration is working to <a href="https://www.notus.org/agencies/trump-administration-yosemite-private-developer-deal">transfer part of Yosemite National Park</a> to a private land developer have heightened <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2025/may/12/trump-is-laying-the-groundwork-to-privatize-americas-national-parks">concerns among park advocates and the public</a> about privatization of public land.</p>

<p>The proposed deal, which a government spokesperson said <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/28/us/trump-administration-yosemite-private-developer.html">has not been finalized</a>, would involve a land swap: The government would give the developer a small area of the park’s land on which to <a href="https://www.notus.org/agencies/trump-administration-yosemite-private-developer-deal">build a private access road</a> between a proposed resort and the park itself. In exchange, the developer would buy land of similar value near the park, or elsewhere in California, and transfer that land to federal ownership.</p>

<p>Environmental advocates and park staff have worried for more than a year that the administration’s <a href="https://www.deseret.com/the-west/2025/07/14/national-park-service-budget-staffing-cuts-doge-doug-burgum/">cuts to the National Park Service’s budget</a> and staffing would lead to further privatization of the national parks’ land and business operations.</p>

<p>The nation has a long history of similar efforts, including a wildly unpopular 1980 attempt by Reagan administration Interior Secretary James Watt to <a href="https://www.nps.gov/parkhistory/online_books/runte1/epilogue.htm">promote development and expand private concessions</a> in the parks. But debate over using public national park land for private profit dates back more than a century before that.</p>

<p>As I explain in my book, “<a href="https://www.nebraskapress.unl.edu/nebraska/9781496239587/the-mountains-are-calling/">The Mountains Are Calling: Tourists and the Unmaking of Yosemite National Park</a>,” no park has played a more central role in that debate than Yosemite, in California. </p>

<h2>Early concerns</h2>

<p>In early 1864, Central American Steamship Transit Company representative Israel Ward Raymond wrote a letter to John Conness, a U.S. senator from California, <a href="https://www.nps.gov/parkhistory/online_books/runte2/chap2.htm">urging the government to move swiftly</a> to preserve the Yosemite Valley and the Mariposa Grove of giant sequoia trees to prevent them from falling into private hands. Five months later, President Abraham Lincoln signed the Yosemite Grant Act, ceding the valley and the grove to the state of California, “upon the express conditions that the premises shall be <a href="https://www.loc.gov/item/today-in-history/june-30/">held for public use, resort, and recreation</a>.” This was years before Yellowstone became the <a href="https://www.archives.gov/milestone-documents/act-establishing-yellowstone-national-park">first federal land designated a national park</a> in 1872.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/680971/original/file-20250718-56-bfyfbq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A sepia-toned image of a lake with massive trees and even bigger mountains behind it." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/680971/original/file-20250718-56-bfyfbq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/680971/original/file-20250718-56-bfyfbq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=548&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/680971/original/file-20250718-56-bfyfbq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=548&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/680971/original/file-20250718-56-bfyfbq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=548&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/680971/original/file-20250718-56-bfyfbq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=688&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/680971/original/file-20250718-56-bfyfbq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=688&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/680971/original/file-20250718-56-bfyfbq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=688&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">For centuries, the natural beauty of the Yosemite Valley has impressed visitors.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/yosemite-national-park-california-circa-1878-albumen-news-photo/1184367836">Sepia Times/Universal Images Group via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Controversy arose quickly at Yosemite. Two men – James Lamon and James Hutchings – had <a href="https://www.nps.gov/parkhistory/online_books/runte2/chap2.htm">claimed land in the valley</a> before the federal government gave it to California. Both began commercial operations, <a href="https://home.nps.gov/yose/blogs/the-first-pioneer-settler-of-yosemite-valley.htm">Lamon growing cash crops</a> and <a href="https://www.nps.gov/yose/learn/historyculture/hutchings.htm">Hutchings operating a hotel</a>.</p>

<p>California said their businesses threatened the state’s ability to develop roads and trails in Yosemite by competing for tourist dollars. A legal battle ensued and was not resolved until an <a href="https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/82/77/">1872 U.S. Supreme Court ruling</a> found that the men’s land claims had not been fully validated according to the procedures of the time. The California legislature <a href="https://home.nps.gov/yose/blogs/the-first-pioneer-settler-of-yosemite-valley.htm">paid both men compensation for their land</a>, and both left the park.</p>

<p>In 1890, <a href="https://www.nps.gov/yose/learn/news/yosemite-national-park-commemorates-its-125th-anniversary.htm?fullweb=1">neighboring parts of the Yosemite area</a> became America’s third national park – and in 1906, the federal government again took possession of the Yosemite Valley itself and the Mariposa Grove, specifically to <a href="https://www.nps.gov/yose/learn/historyculture/thenandnow.htm">incorporate them into an expansion of the national park</a>.</p>

<h2>Development rights</h2>

<p>Yet, as my research has found, the role of private interests in the park remained unsolved. Private companies under contract to the National Park Service have long provided needed amenities <a href="https://www.nps.gov/subjects/concessions/index.htm">such as lodging and food</a> within the national parks. But questions over what is acceptable in national parks in the pursuit of profit have shaped Yosemite’s history for generations.</p>

<p>In 1925, I found, the question centered on the right to build the first gas station inside the park, in Yosemite Valley. Two private businesses, the Curry Camping Company and the Yosemite National Park Company, had long competed for tourist dollars within the park. Each wanted to build a gas station to boost profits.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/680967/original/file-20250718-66-ab4lx0.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C759%2C7659%2C4308&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A large building stands in front of a massive set of cliffs." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/680967/original/file-20250718-66-ab4lx0.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C759%2C7659%2C4308&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/680967/original/file-20250718-66-ab4lx0.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=457&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/680967/original/file-20250718-66-ab4lx0.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=457&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/680967/original/file-20250718-66-ab4lx0.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=457&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/680967/original/file-20250718-66-ab4lx0.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=574&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/680967/original/file-20250718-66-ab4lx0.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=574&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/680967/original/file-20250718-66-ab4lx0.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=574&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">The Ahwahnee is a privately run hotel inside Yosemite National Park.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/construction-crews-at-yosemite-valleys-historic-ahwahnee-news-photo/2207996803">George Rose/Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p><a href="https://npshistory.com/publications/yose/camp_curry_clr.pdf#page=187">Frustrated over the need to decide</a>, National Park Service Director Horace Albright ordered the rival firms to simplify management of the park’s concessions. The companies merged, and the newly formed Yosemite Park and Curry Company was granted the exclusive rights to run lodges, restaurants and other facilities within the park, including the new gas station.</p>

<p>But as I found in my research, the park service and the concessions company did not always see eye to eye on the purpose of the park. The conflict between profit and preservation is perhaps most clearly illustrated by the construction of a ski area within the park in the early 1930s. The park service initially opposed the development of Badger Pass Ski Area as <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/26555031">not conducive to the national park ideal</a>, but the Yosemite Park and Curry Company insisted it was key to boosting winter use of the park.</p>

<p>In 1973, the Music Corporation of America, an entertainment conglomerate, bought the Yosemite Park and Curry Company. The company already had a tourist attraction operating near Hollywood, where visitors could <a href="https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1990-11-27-fi-5451-story.html">pay to tour movie sets</a>, but had not yet changed its name to Universal Studios or launched major theme parks in Florida and California. Its purchase of the park’s concessions set off a <a href="https://www.sierraclub.org/sierra/1974-october">firestorm of controversy</a> over fears of turning Yosemite into a theme park.</p>

<p>That didn’t happen, but annual park visitor numbers climbed <a href="https://irma.nps.gov/Stats/SSRSReports/Park%20Specific%20Reports/Annual%20Park%20Recreation%20Visitation%20Graph%20(1904%20-%20Last%20Calendar%20Year)?Park=YOSE">from 2.5 million to 3.8 million</a> over the 20 years MCA ran the concessions, which sparked concerns about development and overcrowding in the park. Conservationists argued the park service had allowed the corporate giant to promote and develop the park in ways that threatened the very <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/26555031">aspects of the park most people came to enjoy</a>.</p>

<p>With three restaurants, two service stations with a total of 15 gas pumps, two cafeterias, two grocery stores, seven souvenir shops, a delicatessen, a bank, a skating rink, three swimming pools, a golf course, two tennis courts, kennels, a barbershop, a beauty shop, Badger Pass Ski Area and three lodges, the Yosemite Valley was a <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/26555031">busy commercial district</a>. Critics argued that such development contradicted the park service’s mandate to leave national parks <a href="https://www.nps.gov/aboutus/index.htm">unimpaired for the enjoyment of future generations</a>.</p>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Who owns the names?</h2>

<p>Falling profits and consolidation within the music industry led MCA to sell its concessions rights in Yosemite in 1993. The Delaware North Companies, a global hospitality corporation, took over and <a href="https://www.kvpr.org/business-economy/2015-06-17/longtime-yosemite-concessionaire-is-out-as-nps-selects-aramark">ran the park’s concessions</a> until 2016, when it sold the rights to Aramark.</p>

<p>But in that sale, the question of public resources and private profits arose again. Delaware North <a href="https://niagarafallsreporter.com/delaware-north-loses-yosemite-contract-can-niagara-falls-state-park-be-next-2/">demanded $51 million in compensation</a> for Aramark continuing to use the names of several historic properties within the park, such as the <a href="https://www.nps.gov/places/000/the-ahwahnee.htm">Ahwahnee, a hotel</a>, and <a href="https://www.nps.gov/places/000/curry-village.htm">Curry Village</a>, another group of visitor accommodations. The company claimed those names were a part of its assets under its contract with the park service.</p>

<p>The park service rejected the claim, saying the names, which dated back more than a century, belonged to the American people. But to avoid legal problems during the transition, the <a href="https://www.nps.gov/yose/learn/news/yosemite-national-park-to-change-historic-property-names.htm">agency temporarily renamed several sites</a>, including calling the Ahwahnee the Majestic Yosemite Hotel and changing Curry Village to Half Dome Village. Public outrage erupted, denouncing the claim by Delaware North as <a href="https://boomcalifornia.org/2016/06/16/yosemite-by-any-name-is-still-the-peoples-park/">commercial overreach</a> that threatened to distort Yosemite’s heritage. In 2019, the park service and Aramark agreed to pay Delaware North a <a href="https://www.npr.org/2019/07/16/742081777/yosemite-hotels-get-their-historic-names-back-after-trademark-dispute">total of $12 million</a> to settle the dispute, and the original names were restored.</p>

            <figcaption><span class="caption">Protesters unfurl an upside-down U.S. flag from the top of El Capitan in Yosemite National Park in February 2025, protesting Trump administration changes to the National Park Service.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Renewed interest in commercial efforts</h2>

<p>In June 2025, Yosemite again took center stage in the dispute over the role of federal funding versus private interests at the start of the second Trump administration when a group of climbers unfurled an <a href="https://www.cpr.org/2025/06/12/trump-budget-impact-national-parks-concerns/">American flag upside down off El Capitan</a> in protest of the administration’s cuts in personnel and slashing of the park service’s budget. </p>

<p>Conservationists, including former National Park Service Director Jonathan Jarvis, argued that by <a href="https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/nation/2025/05/04/trump-budget-proposal-cuts-to-parks/83428514007/">defunding the park service</a> and laying off as much as a <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2025/07/03/us/politics/park-service-staffing.html">quarter of its workforce</a>, the Trump administration was “<a href="https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2025/may/12/trump-is-laying-the-groundwork-to-privatize-americas-national-parks">laying the groundwork to privatize” the national parks</a> by allowing <a href="https://grist.org/climate/the-trump-administrations-push-to-privatize-us-public-lands/">corporate interests more access to public lands</a>. Those concerns echo ones raised during the first Trump administration, when the White House argued <a href="https://perma.cc/JQN5-Z8TL">privatization would better serve the American public</a> by improving visitor experiences and saving federal dollars. </p>

<p>Members of Congress and former park service officials say the reported effort in 2026 to turn over park land to a private owner would be a <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/28/us/trump-administration-yosemite-private-developer.html">major blow to federal efforts to protect parks</a> and conserve land.</p>

<p>Whichever side prevails in the short term, the debate over the role of private interests within national parks like Yosemite will undoubtedly continue.</p>

<title>Decades after 9/11, toxic dust and PTSD may be accelerating brain aging among first responders</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757070/original/file-20260831-50-fxel1p.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C1024%2C682&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">The aftermath of the World Trade Center attacks casts a long shadow on survivors.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/firefighters-gather-by-the-south-reflecting-pool-during-the-news-photo/2234175241">Adam Gray/Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Hundreds of first responders have told me they remember exactly how they felt during the World Trade Center attacks, even 25 years on.</p>

<p>They tell me that they remember not being able to think, see or smell anything. They could focus only on digging and pulling debris out of the way. They could not rest because those trapped beneath the rubble could not wait. Death was all around them, and they could only do as much as they could to hold it back.</p>

<p>While what happened on 9/11 was unprecedented, similar tragedies happen quite frequently. As a <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=3axQJv8AAAAJ&amp;hl=en">physician in occupational health</a> who works with 9/11 first responders, I can easily imagine those same thoughts from other firefighters, paramedics and construction workers trying to save lives after the deadly summer 2026 earthquakes in <a href="https://theconversation.com/earthquakes-in-venezuela-expose-a-severely-under-resourced-and-unprepared-healthcare-system-287003">Venezuela</a>, <a href="https://theconversation.com/colombia-earthquake-has-killed-at-least-132-my-research-helps-explain-why-it-was-so-destructive-289478">Colombia</a> and <a href="https://apnews.com/article/indonesia-earthquake-magnitude-77-c31ad3cf07fa83d2d443e8d85e5c9d84">Indonesia</a> or the disastrous <a href="https://theconversation.com/nepals-flash-floods-show-the-devastating-power-of-cascading-hazards-290611">floods in Nepal</a>. </p>

<p>These first responders may also need to recover human remains from the rubble. Surrounding these moments of intimate grief are dust, toxic fumes and cries for help. And this trauma takes a toll.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757075/original/file-20260831-50-be7gu1.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Aerial view of the wreckage of the World Trade Center, crowds of first responders attempting to rescue and recover survivors from the rubble" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757075/original/file-20260831-50-be7gu1.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757075/original/file-20260831-50-be7gu1.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=402&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757075/original/file-20260831-50-be7gu1.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=402&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757075/original/file-20260831-50-be7gu1.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=402&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757075/original/file-20260831-50-be7gu1.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=505&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757075/original/file-20260831-50-be7gu1.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=505&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757075/original/file-20260831-50-be7gu1.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=505&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">The destruction of the World Trade Center was unprecedented, but such disasters are not uncommon throughout the world.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/rescue-workers-sift-through-the-wreckage-of-the-world-trade-news-photo/1339510">Mario Tama/Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Whether it’s industrial or nuclear disasters, extreme weather, wildfires, volcanic eruptions, war or terrorist attacks, first responders and affected communities can experience <a href="https://doi.org/10.1017/s1049023x19000141">significant physical and mental health effects</a> both during rescue and recovery operations and for years afterward. All are vulnerable to mental and physical harm no matter how well trained they may be. </p>

<p>Research from my team suggests that among these risks is post-traumatic stress disorder that may <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41398-025-03769-7">cause their brain to age faster</a>.</p>

<h2>PTSD among first responders</h2>

<p><a href="https://theconversation.com/acute-stress-and-early-signs-of-ptsd-are-common-in-firefighters-and-other-first-responders-heres-what-to-watch-out-for-247365">Post-traumatic stress disorder, also known as PTSD</a>, is a complex mental health condition that can develop after experiencing or witnessing a traumatic event. <a href="https://theconversation.com/what-is-trauma-the-more-we-talk-about-it-the-more-it-means-279754">Psychological trauma</a> refers to the lasting emotional effects of direct or indirect exposure to life-threatening circumstances or violence. </p>

<p>PTSD may involve intrusive memories, avoidance, heightened alertness, sleep problems and changes in mood and thinking. Anxiety and depression commonly occur alongside PTSD.</p>

<p>Around 23% of World Trade Center responders <a href="https://doi.org/10.1017/s003329171100256x">have been diagnosed with PTSD</a>. In comparison, around 6% of the U.S. general population are <a href="https://www.ptsd.va.gov/professional/treat/essentials/epidemiology.asp">estimated to have had PTSD</a> over their lifetime.</p>

<p>When I talk to 9/11 first responders, they describe their PTSD and cognitive difficulties as interconnected problems that continue to affect their lives today. Those traumatic memories remain vivid, and some first responders continue to experience anxiety, depression, intrusive thoughts, sleep problems and difficulty controlling their emotions. </p>

<h2>Trauma speeds brain aging</h2>

<p>As they age, many 9/11 first responders have also noticed their memory, concentration and mental sharpness get worse. They increasingly fear losing their independence. Rather than occurring as separate conditions, physical illness, cognitive changes and emotional distress <a href="https://doi.org/10.1002/jts.22631">often reinforce one another</a>. </p>

<p>In another study, researchers from my team monitored the cognitive function of more than 5,000 World Trade Center first responders without dementia between 2014 and 2022. Over approximately five years, 228 developed dementia before age 65. First responders with the most severe exposure to potentially <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41582-021-00576-8">neurotoxic dust and debris at ground zero</a> had a substantially <a href="https://doi.org/10.1002/alz.089161">higher incidence of dementia</a> than those with minimal exposure or who consistently used personal protective equipment such as respirators. This link remained after controlling for demographic, lifestyle, medical and genetic factors.</p>

<p>Before I began studying the health effects of 9/11, I was examining workers exposed to <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.shaw.2021.12.906">neurotoxic metals and industrial pollution</a> in northern Italy. Knowing the harmful toxins in World Trade Center dust, I began to wonder whether 9/11 responders might face similar long-term risks to their brains. That concern grew when brain scans of both groups showed a similar <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/bs.ant.2022.05.002">increase in deposits</a> of a protein linked to Alzheimer’s disease and cognitive decline called <a href="https://theconversation.com/alzheimers-disease-is-partly-genetic-studying-the-genes-that-delay-decline-in-some-may-lead-to-treatments-for-all-205914">beta-amyloid</a>.</p>

            </figcaption>

<p>Research from my team also found that the brains of 9/11 male responders with PTSD had <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41398-025-03769-7">MRI results consistent with older-appearing brains</a> than those without PTSD. </p>

<p>In that 2025 study, we measured the brain structures using MRI scans and an AI model to estimate each participant’s brain age. The AI model had been trained to predict a person’s chronological age from the overall structure of their brain, based on data from more than 11,500 MRI brain scans from healthy people ages 5 to 95. We used the difference between a person’s predicted brain age and their actual age as a measure of accelerated brain aging. </p>

<p>We also saw that first responders with PTSD had brains that appeared about <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41398-025-03769-7">three years older</a> than their chronological age. In contrast, the estimated brain age of responders without PTSD approximately matched their actual chronological age. Each additional month a first responder spent working at ground zero was associated with roughly four to five additional months of apparent brain aging, suggesting that how long they were exposed to the disaster played a key role in this aging process.</p>

<p>The experiences of first responders show that the effects of 9/11 are an ongoing health issue. These health consequences evolve as people age, and they still require coordinated mental, cognitive, physical and social support decades later.</p>

<p>Every 9/11 anniversary brings back vivid memories of the tragedy, along with the same restlessness, frustration and pain of being there. Yet many on the front lines have told me that they feel pride and a sense of belonging with the knowledge that they helped people in desperate need. Their service remains an enduring example of human solidarity in a moment of crisis.</p>

<p>Honoring that legacy also means protecting those who come to our rescue during the emergency. I believe that, as a society, Americans have a responsibility to safeguard, protect and care for their health throughout their entire lives. They were there for America in one of its darkest moments; Americans must be there for them in the years to come.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/289755/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />
